docs.title: How Coimbra Shaped West-East Connections
docs.text:
Notes on the relationship between Coimbra, Portugal, and China, focusing on Jesuit missions.

Coimbra was the site of the first Jesuit college, established in 1543. It was created with the specific purpose of training future missionaries to the East.

With an endowment for 200 students, it was to be the primary recruitment center for missionaries destined for China.

Since 1537, King John III of Portugal was developing in Coimbra a university intended to be one of the best in Europe. Mobilising significant financial resources and pressing bishops and religious orders to join the project, the king transformed the city, building new colleges and repurposing the former royal palace as the center of academic life. Some of the best professors were hired for Coimbra, and later a preparatory school was created to prepare future university students.

The king's goal? To produce the much-needed human resources for his expanding overseas possessions and to staff the many instances where matters of faith and church were crucial for the fostering of Portugal's interests in the global stage.

This goal intersected with the path of a small group of graduates of the University of Paris who in 1534 had sworn to defend the christian faith and obediance to the Pope, creating the seed of what would quickly become one the most remarkable global organizations in history: the Jesuits.

Coimbra and the emergence of the Chinese missions

Mattteo Ricci and Coimbra

docs.title: Diogo Gouveia   the "fixer", Paris, and the birth of the Eastern Jesuit Missions
docs.text:
Francis Xavier died in the island of Shangshuan in December of 1552, as he waited an opportunity to enter China.

He would later become a Saint and represents to this day the archetype of the Jesuit missionary in the East. One of the founders of the Society and the organizer of the Jesuit first and most spectacular overseas operation. He alone made the Society transition from a group of devoted young men to a global organization which shaped the future of the world in many aspects.

But how this came to be? How was it possible? To ask a simpler question: how far back in the history of Francis and his mates must we go to find a plausible seed moment from which this enormous tree grew.

We need to go back to Paris, to the Quartier Latin, in the years 1520. More specifically to the Collége de Sainte Barbare, where young Francis met for the first time those who will shape his future. The people he met, the place where they met and the web of connections around that place, constitute the basic plumbing that will conduct the energy of the vast systemic changes that were taking place at the time.

This is a story with many angles and many points of view. Here we will focus first on the point of view of Diogo de Gouveia, the Elder, head of the college, former rector of the Sorbonne and the french fixer of Portuguese king John the III. In Gouveia's college, Francis, Inácio de Loyola, Simão Rodrigues and Pedro Fabro met. They would become the core of the future society.

Diogo came to Paris as a student, probably in 1492, with a grant from the Portuguese king John the II and later from king Manuel II. From 1513 onwards, in his early 40's he is on record writing to the portuguese king about deals related to french corsairs, a complex system of attacks, ransoms, and compensations. For years Gouveia will be the fixer of the multiple incidents that french corsairs created in the newly sea routes to Brasil and the East operated by Portuguese ships. In 1520 he takes charge of the College of Santa Barbara. Santa Bárbara was one of the colleges surrounding the University of Paris. Created in 1460 as a "private" college by a professor of the university it had changed hands in 1512, bought by the owner of another college. In 1520 Gouveia rents the college.

Colleges were a good business in Paris, like in other university cities of the time.The model is simple to understand. In order to enter university students had to learn latin and get the basic preparatory education. Also, during their life as university students, they needed a place to stay and study. So colleges provided the living and learning environment, together with discipline and preparatory courses. These courses could be rather sofisticated and a college would compete with others with the quality of the resident professors.

Gouveia had a pretty competitive operation. But, more importantly, he had a steady source of income: the portuguese students sent to Paris

docs.title: Mattteo Ricci and Coimbra
docs.text:
Matteo Ricci was in Coimbra from June 1577 until his departure to India in March 1578.

This stay of a few months at the jesuit College in Coimbra was common.

Recruits for the Indian missions would travel to Portugal to board the fleet that every year departed from Lisbon to Goa around March-Abril. If they arrived too late to depart that year they would have to wait for the next departure.

Coimbra was a natural place to spend the waiting time. The jesuit college was created in 1543, by King John III, specifically to train the missionaries for the Eastern missions. The college was one of several that were built in Coimbra after 1537, when the Portuguese university was transferred from Lisbon to Coimbra.

docs.title: The Emergence of Coimbra as the Primary Center for Eastern Missions in the 16th Century
Introduction
docs.text: This overview originated from an effort to document and analyze the historical connections between Coimbra and the Eastern missions, with particular emphasis on the Jesuit missionary enterprise in China. The investigation reveals a complex network of causal relationships that positioned Coimbra as a pivotal center for global missionary activities in the East.

docs.title: Historical Context and Causal Factors
docs.text:
A preliminary analysis identifies several critical factors that converged to establish Coimbra's central role:

  • The convergence of key figures including Ignatius of Loyola, Francis Xavier, and Simão Rodrigues at the Colégio de Santa Bárbara during the 1530s
  • The multifaceted contributions of Diogo Gouveia, who served simultaneously as College Director, Royal Envoy, and administrator of a scholarship fund that facilitated the education of numerous promising individuals
  • The geopolitical impasse created by conflict in the Levant, which obstructed traditional pilgrimage routes to the Holy Land and kept the first Jesuits in Italy
  • Diogo Gouveia's correspondence with the Portuguese king concerning financing of studies, wherein he referenced Francis I's methods for accessing ecclesiastical resources and proposed inviting the Jesuits to undertake missionary work in Portuguese territories
  • King João III's ambitious educational project for Coimbra
  • The selection of Francis Xavier and Simão Rodrigues by Inacius Loyola for Eastern missions
  • The consequential decision to deploy one missionary while retaining the other to establish the Coimbra college, which would function as the "seminary of the East"—a Solomonic resolution with profound implications for the evolution of Jesuit missionary enterprise.

docs.title: Institutional Development and Global Impact
docs.text:
These interconnected historical developments elucidate the presence of a Coimbra-educated student in Canton attempting to establish the inaugural mission in China in 1555, preceding even the Portuguese settlement of Macau (Melchior Nunes Barreto)

Further examination of this intricate network of relationships and causal mechanisms, centered around a compact group of influential figures (Loyola, Simão Rodrigues, Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, along with the initial rectors in Coimbra, King João III, and Prince Henry), demonstrates Coimbra's structural role in the definition, shaping and staffing of Jesuit missions in the East

Coimbra represented the first instance where the Society of Jesus confronted the implications of large-scale recruitment of academically trained youth, including individuals from elite noble backgrounds. This development was facilitated by Coimbra's substantial institutional resources: the Crown established the college with a capacity for 200 students, indicating from its inception a global rather than national educational mandate.

The college's strategic location adjacent to the University of Coimbra provided access to a substantial pool of potential recruits. Consequently, Coimbra became the primary site for addressing fundamental organizational challenges: the theological and practical considerations of religious vows, questions of institutional scale, competition and opposition from established religious orders, familial resistance to religious vocations, the complexities of maintaining rigorous academic standards, and the moderation of ascetic excesses among those remaining in academic roles rather than pursuing missionary work abroad.

Furthermore, Coimbra witnessed the emergence of another transformative process that fundamentally shaped Jesuit development: the assumption of administrative responsibility for the Colégio das Artes in 1555, occurring three years after Francis Xavier's death in Sanchuan. This institutional acquisition, reportedly resisted by Loyola over an extended period, would exert global influence on Jesuit educational and missionary strategies and generate the famous Conimbricenses textbooks used as reference for the diffusion of the Western scientific tradition in China.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: The historical evidence demonstrates an interconnected institutional evolution. The Crown's directive proved compelling, though the process involved significant deliberation and temporary reversals, including the Jesuits' initial relinquishment of the college, which temporarily reverted to the Hieronymite order before final consolidation under Jesuit administration.

docs.title: "Release early, release often"
docs.text:
Release early, release often is the famous software development philosophy promoted by Eric Raymond.

As I struggle with the huge amount of information related the Jesuit mission in China, I am borrowing this from the Cathedral and the Bazaar in the hope of breaking the writer's paralysis.

The aim is to write quickly short synthesis, and iterate and improve frequently.
